Groups of 30: frequent ketamine use (more than four times a week), infrequent use (less than four times a week but at least once a month), ex-ketamine (abstinent for at least 1 month), polydrug and non-drug controls. Family history of mental illness was more common in the frequent group (8 of 30 against 2, 3, 1 and 1 in the other groups; χ²(4) = 12.59, P = 0.013), with no first-degree relative with schizophrenia in any group, and the frequent group had 12.27 (4.84) years of education against 14.23 to 15.33. The authors state that pre-existing differences cannot be ruled out, that the family history may have contributed to the findings, and that childhood trauma, a risk factor for dissociation, was not measured.

Of the same participants, 25 of the 30 in the frequent group were retested (mean interval for all retested participants 366.6 (92.11) days); reported ketamine use changed little (no effect of time; 16.0 (10.01) days a month at follow-up, 22 of 25 still using at least monthly). Averaged over both sessions the frequent group still made more spatial working-memory errors than all other groups (group F(4,108) = 4.16, printed P = 0.04) and recognised fewer patterns than the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups (printed F(1,108) = 4.429, P = 0.002), but its errors fell from 29.58 (19.93) to 19.92 (17.56), against 11.48 to 18.32 at the first session and 12.48 to 15.89 a year later in the other groups, and its pattern recognition rose from 83.68% (10.27) to 89.04% (7.24), against 88.41% (polydrug) and 89.58% (non-drug) at follow-up; its strategy score improved (31.63 to 27.33, P = 0.003) and its Stockings score rose from 7.67 to 9.50 (P = 0.003), inside the other groups' follow-up range (9.33 to 9.87); story recall showed no group effects.
